content: Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250, also known as I.42655, is a blue dye frequently utilized in sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). During the staining process, the gel is immersed in the dye for approximately 30 minutes, followed by a destaining step lasting 30 minutes or longer. This procedure enables the visualization of protein bands within the gel, which represent the protein content. Typically, the gel includes molecular weight markers—proteins of known molecular weights—allowing for the determination of the molecular weight of proteins in an unknown solution during visualization. A variation of this dye, Coomassie G-250, is shown on the right. Another similar but distinct dye, Coomassie R-250, also exists. Coomassie dye plays a critical role in the Bradford Method, a widely used technique for quantifying protein concentration in a solution. The dye binds to proteins through physical adsorption to specific amino acid residues, including arginine, aromatic amino acids, and histidine. When Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 binds to proteins in an acidic solution, its absorbance shifts from 465 nm to 595 nm. This absorbance data can be applied to Beer’s Law to calculate the protein concentration, ultimately determining the total amount of protein in the solution. For staining, specific solutions are prepared, and destaining can be achieved using distilled water and heating, although this method is slower. Methanol, historically used in these processes, can be replaced with ethanol to create safer reagents, as methanol is a neurotoxin. The substitution does not compromise the efficiency of the procedure. The name Coomassie originates from the city of Kumasi, located in present-day Ghana. The dye was initially developed as an acid wool dye and was named to commemorate the British occupation of the Ashanti capital, then known as Coomassie, in 1896.
